system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 19 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-02-20 00:17:00 to 2174-03-10 15:36:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with a five-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the back and nonbloody emesis, consistent with an acute exacerbation. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN infusion via her existing PICC line, and symptom control using IV hydromorphone and ondansetron. Her pain and nausea gradually improved, allowing transition to oral medications and a soft diet by hospital day 6. She was started on oral vitamin B12 due to borderline low levels, and impacted cerumen was identified in the right ear, with instructions to avoid self-cleaning and follow up with her PCP or ENT. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans for close GI follow-up to manage TPN discontinuation, nutritional lab monitoring, and iron supplementation as an outpatient.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

radiology_notes.text:
AP CHEST, 4:22 A.M., ___

HISTORY:  ___ woman with indwelling PICC line.  Please localize.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Left PIC line ends in the mid-to-low SVC, unchanged.  Lungs are clear,
cardiomediastinal and hilar silhouettes and pleural surfaces are normal.

HISTORY:  Chronic pancreatitis, admitted with acute pancreatitis with new pain
in right lower quadrant, more likely a complication of pancreatitis such as a
pseudocyst, clinically unlikely to represent appendicitis.  Rule out
complications of pancreatitis and appendicitis.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial helical MDCT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed prior
to and after the administration of intravenous contrast.

Multiplanar sagittal and coronal reformatted images were generated.  DLP: 
1446.40 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  This study is compared to prior MRCP from ___ and prior
CT abdomen from ___.

FINDINGS:

CT ABDOMEN:  
There is a 3-mm nodule in the right middle lobe (3:4), stable.  There is a
calcified 3-mm granuloma in the right lower lobe (7:14).  There are minimal
dependent atelectatic changes at the right lung base.  The heart is not
enlarged.

The pancreas is slightly atrophic, in keeping with known chronic pancreatitis.
In addition, there is an equivocal amount of fat stranding surrounding the
head and uncinate process of the pancreas which may could correlate with acute
pancreatitis.  There is a small 6 mm hypodense lesion within the body of the
pancreas (3:21) which likely corresponds to a chronically dilated side branch
related to chronic pancreatitis, similar to previous MRCP.  There has been
prior cholecystectomy.  There is a small amount of pneumobilia.  There is a
right renal cyst with a thin septation.  The spleen, adrenal glands, left
kidney appear unremarkable.  Incidental note is made of a circumaortic left
renal vein.  There is a small hiatal hernia.  The abdominal aorta and major
branch vessels appear unremarkable without aneurysm or dissection.  The
appendix is not definitely visualized within the right lower quadrant;
however, there are no inflammatory changes to suggest acute appendicitis.  The
small bowel appears unremarkable.  There is no intra-abdominal or
retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  There is no ascites.  There is a small
hiatal hernia. 

CT PELVIS:  
The bladder appears unremarkable.  There are subcutaneous areas of fat
stranding and gas in the anterior abdominal wall, likely from injection sites.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:
There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic bone lesions.  There is partial
fusion of T10 and T11 which may be congenital.  There are probable bilateral
perineural cysts noted within the sacrum.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Atrophic pancreas compatible with chronic pancreatitis.  No definite
evidence for superimposed acute pancreatitis, though an equivocal amount of
fat stranding may be present about the head and uncinate process of the
pancreas that could correlate with acute pancreatitis if the clinical picture
suggests this.  

2.  Appendix was not visualized; however, no findings to suggest acute
appendicitis.

procedures.long_title: Parenteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s that same pain I always get—epigastric, radiating to my back. It’s been going on for about 48 hours now. Worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. You were given some Dilaudid and Zofran in the ER. Are you feeling any relief?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but it still hurts, especially when I breathe deeply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll keep managing your pain. You’re on your fentanyl patch, and we’ll add IV Dilaudid as needed. We’re also starting TPN through your PICC line since you need to rest your bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been doing TPN at home three times a week, depending on how much I can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll continue that. We also checked labs. Your hemoglobin is low at 8.6, and your ferritin is only 5.0, which means you’re severely iron deficient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. I knew I was anemic, but I didn’t know it was that low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV iron during your stay—three doses—and start you on oral iron tablets to take daily after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Should I be worried about where the iron loss is coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s important. Since you’re post-menopausal, we recommend a colonoscopy to check for any sources of bleeding. Please follow up with your PCP about scheduling it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had one a few years ago, but I guess it’s time for another. I’ll call them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your B12 was low last time, but it’s now normal at 264. We’ll keep you on your multivitamin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I’ve been taking it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray early this morning. Your PICC line is still in the right place, and your lungs are clear. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might have moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. I haven’t eaten, so that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now. Your lipase is only 30, which is normal, but your symptoms and history point to pancreatitis. The CT scan shows an atrophic pancreas, consistent with chronic disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not acute? I thought the pain was worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s called acute on chronic pancreatitis. The CT shows some fat stranding that could suggest acute inflammation, but it’s not definitive. Your clinical picture supports a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. So same treatment as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. TPN, pain control, and slow progression to food when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count is low at 4.2, and it’s dropping. But it’s been like this in the past, so we think it’s chronic pancytopenia, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Should we do anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s stable, and you’re not showing signs of infection. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned new pain in your right lower quadrant. We did a CT to check for complications like a pseudocyst or appendicitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been bothering me. Could it be a pseudocyst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan didn’t show any pseudocyst or abscess. The appendix wasn’t seen, but there are no signs of inflammation. It’s likely referred pain from your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried it might be something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you the second dose of IV iron this morning. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not vomiting. I’ve been using the ondansetron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that available. Also, you’re still constipated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, even with the senna and docusate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can add a Dulcolax if needed. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving, and you’ve been stable. We’d like to start you on clear liquids today—water, broth, apple juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I miss tasting food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance your diet gradually. We’ll also reduce your IV pain meds and rely more on your oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on 8 mg every 3 hours. Will that change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to every 6 hours as needed. You’ll still have the fentanyl patch on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on clear liquids. Today, we’ll try a full liquid diet—yogurt, pudding, cream of wheat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid fatty foods. Stick to low-fat, bland options. And continue avoiding alcohol, of course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had alcohol in years. I know it’s bad for my pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your kidney function is slightly worse—BUN up to 22, creatinine 1.0. But it’s likely from mild dehydration. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s a small change, and you’re improving overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you in a few days. You’ll go home on TPN, your usual pain meds, and the new oral iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I live far from the hospital, so phone visits with my GI doctor help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. Make sure to keep those appointments. Also, follow up with your PCP about the colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated a soft diet well. No nausea or pain flares. We’ll keep preparing for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. I just hope this doesn’t happen again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to prevent that. Continue your TPN as scheduled, avoid fatty foods, and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll be discharged tomorrow. You’re on clear liquids, pain is controlled, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual meds: bupropion, sertraline, trazodone, oxybutynin, PPI, ranitidine, stool softeners, and Excedrin for migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ferrous sulfate daily for iron, and we’ve given you 40 doses of Dilaudid 8 mg to take every 6 hours as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. A nurse will go over your TPN instructions and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check. You’re alert, walking, eating clear liquids, and pain is manageable. We’re confident you can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll follow up with my doctors like we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll continue TPN at home, take your iron daily, and monitor for any return of pain or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if it gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep your follow-up appointments. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with acute on chronic pancreatitis, presenting with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and recent weight loss. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN via her existing PICC line, and IV hydromorphone, later transitioning to oral pain medications. Imaging showed an atrophic pancreas with equivocal findings for acute inflammation, consistent with a flare. She gradually improved over 19 days, tolerating clear liquids by discharge. During her stay, she received three doses of IV iron for severe iron deficiency anemia and was started on oral iron supplementation, with a recommendation to follow up with her PCP for a colonoscopy. Her chronic pancytopenia remained stable, and B12 levels were normal. She was discharged home on her prior pain regimen, TPN, and updated medications including daily ferrous sulfate, with plans for ongoing outpatient management.
